units.title: Energy and Chemical Reactions
units.intro: Energy is conserved. In chemistry we track heat. Breaking bonds *takes* energy (endothermic). Making bonds *releases* energy (exothermic). The sign of the whole reaction is which side wins.

cards.title: You still climb Ea even when the landing is lower — that is why cold petrol does not burst into flame by itself.
5.1.1 Law of Conservation of Energy
body: All matter possesses energy in one form or another.
The different forms of kinetic energy include thermal energy and electrical energy.
The different forms of potential energy include chemical energy and gravitational energy.
The most common form of energy change in chemical reactions is heat change, and thus the major part of this sub-unit will be concerned with the heat changes that accompany chemical reactions.

cards.title: 5.1.3 Bond Breaking and Bond Formation
body: Chemical reactions usually involve the making or breaking of chemical bonds.
The energy of the product molecules may therefore be greater or less than the energy of the reactant molecules.

cards.title: 5.1.4 Enthalpy and ΔH, step by step
body: Every substance stores energy in its bonds. The **heat content** of a substance at constant pressure is called its **enthalpy, H**. We cannot measure H itself, but we can measure the **change**, ΔH (“delta H”), during a reaction.
$$\Delta H = H_{\text{products}} - H_{\text{reactants}} = H_P - H_R$$
**Step 1 — Bonds in the reactants are broken.** This never happens by itself: energy must be **supplied** (absorbed), so this stage is endothermic.
**Step 2 — New bonds in the products are formed.** This happens by itself and energy is **released**, so this stage is exothermic.
**Step 3 — Compare the two amounts:**
$$\Delta H = \sum(\text{energy to break bonds}) - \sum(\text{energy released forming bonds})$$
If more energy is released than absorbed, ΔH is **negative** (exothermic, H_P < H_R). If more is absorbed, ΔH is **positive** (endothermic, H_P > H_R).
**Unit:** kilojoules per mole, **kJ/mol** — per mole of reaction as written in the equation.
**Activity 5.5 explained:** adding quicklime (CaO) to water makes the beaker hot. Heat flows **from the beaker to your hand**: the reaction CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ releases energy, so ΔH is negative.

cards.title: Model: break bonds, then make bonds (H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl)

steps.text: **Break:** H–H (436 kJ) and Cl–Cl (243 kJ) need 679 kJ in total — the energy goes **up** to separate atoms.
**Make:** two H–Cl bonds form (2 × 432 = 864 kJ) — energy comes **out**.
**Net:** ΔH = 679 − 864 = **−185 kJ** per mole of reaction: the products are lower, the reaction is exothermic.

cards.title: Tips and common mistakes
body: ΔH = (bonds broken) − (bonds formed) — reactant bonds first. Do not reverse it.
Count every bond: 2NH₃ has 6 N–H bonds; CO₂ has 2 C=O bonds; 2O₂ has 2 O=O bonds.
Exothermic → negative ΔH, even though “heat is given out”.

cards.title: 5.1.6 Energy-Level Diagrams
body: Energy is supplied to the reactants to raise the particles up to the higher energy level.

cards.title: Exothermic or endothermic? Step by step
body: The **system** is the reacting chemicals; the **surroundings** are everything else (the beaker, the water, the air, your hand).
**Step 1 — Bonds.** Breaking bonds **absorbs** energy; making bonds **releases** energy.
**Step 2 — Compare.** If more energy is released making the new bonds than was absorbed breaking the old ones, the reaction is **exothermic**; otherwise it is **endothermic**.

**Step 3 — Sign of ΔH.** Exothermic: heat leaves the system, **ΔH < 0** (negative), the surroundings get **warmer**. Endothermic: heat enters the system, **ΔH > 0** (positive), the surroundings get **colder**.
$$\Delta H = H_{\text{products}} - H_{\text{reactants}}$$
**Step 4 — Check with a thermometer:** temperature of the mixture rises → exothermic; falls → endothermic.

cards.title: Everyday examples
head: Exothermic (ΔH negative, gets hot)
Endothermic (ΔH positive, gets cold or needs heating)
rows: Burning methane (natural gas), wood, charcoal: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, ΔH = −890 kJ
Respiration in our cells (the reverse of photosynthesis)
Thermal decomposition: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, ΔH = +178 kJ (lime kilns)
Neutralisation: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, ΔH = −57.1 kJ
Dissolving NH₄NO₃ or NH₄Cl in water (instant cold packs)
Slaking quicklime: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (very hot)
Dissolving NaOH or concentrated H₂SO₄ in water
Melting ice, boiling water, sweat evaporating (cools the skin)
Rusting of iron, condensation of steam, freezing of water
Baking soda + vinegar (the mixture feels cold); cooking an egg

steps.text: **Exothermic:** the products are **lower** than the reactants. The drop is ΔH (negative): energy given out.
**Endothermic:** the products are **higher** than the reactants. The rise is ΔH (positive): energy taken in.
**Activation energy, Ea:** from the reactants up to the top of the hump. Even exothermic reactions must climb it first (a match is needed to light gas).
A **catalyst** gives a lower hump (smaller Ea) but does **not** change ΔH.

cards.title: How to draw an energy-level diagram, step by step
body: 1. Draw a vertical axis labelled **energy (enthalpy, H)** and a horizontal axis **reaction progress**.
2. Draw a short line for the **reactants** on the left.
3. Draw the **products** on the right: **lower** for exothermic, **higher** for endothermic. Write the formulas on the lines.
4. Join them with a curve that rises to a **hump** (the activated complex).
5. Add arrows: **Ea** from reactants up to the top of the hump; **ΔH** from reactants to products (pointing down for exothermic, up for endothermic). Write its value with the sign.
**Reverse reaction:** ΔH changes sign, and \(E_a(\text{reverse}) = E_a(\text{forward}) - \Delta H\).

cards.title: Worked example: burning methane
cards.problem: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ/mol. (a) Is it exo- or endothermic? (b) Describe its energy diagram. (c) How much heat is released by burning 8.0 g of methane (M = 16 g/mol)?

steps.text: (b) Products (CO₂ + 2H₂O) are drawn 890 kJ **below** the reactants (CH₄ + 2O₂), with a hump between them; ΔH arrow points down.

cards.title: Worked example: nitrogen monoxide
cards.problem: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), ΔH = +180 kJ. (a) Exo or endo? (b) What is ΔH for 2NO → N₂ + O₂? (c) Why does NO form in a car engine or during lightning but not in ordinary air?

steps.text: (a) ΔH positive → **endothermic**; the products are 180 kJ above the reactants.
(b) The reverse reaction has the opposite sign: ΔH = −180 kJ.
(c) The reaction needs a large energy input (and a high Ea); the very high temperatures in engines and lightning supply it.

cards.answer: Endothermic; reverse ΔH = −180 kJ; needs very high temperature.

cards.title: Worked example: numbers from a diagram
cards.problem: On an energy diagram the reactants are at 50 kJ, the top of the hump at 150 kJ and the products at 20 kJ. Find Ea, ΔH and Ea of the reverse reaction.
cards.answer: Ea = 100 kJ, ΔH = −30 kJ, Ea(reverse) = 130 kJ

cards.title: 5.1.9 Thermochemical Equations
body: An equation that contains the information about the heat changes involved in a reaction is called a **thermochemical equation**.
The physical states of reactants and products should be stated.
The value of ΔH given in kJ/mol refers to the amounts (moles) of reactants and products exactly as written in the equation.

cards.title: 5.2.3 Heat of Neutralization
body: **Heat of neutralization** is the heat released when 1 mol of water is formed during the neutralization of an acid by an alkali.

steps.text: *   Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.
*   Potential energy is stored energy due to position, composition, or chemical bonds.
Chemical energy stored within the molecular bonds of a substance is a form of **potential energy**.

steps.text: The correct relationship is **$$1\text{ calorie} = 4.2\text{ Joules}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What happens thermodynamically when any chemical bond is broken inside a molecule?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define bond breaking energetics**
To break a chemical bond, attractive electrostatic forces between atoms must be physically overcome.

**Step 2: Identify energy direction**
Overcoming these forces requires an input of energy from the surroundings. Thus, bond breaking is always **endothermic** (absorbs energy).

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct choice is **Energy must be absorbed (endothermic).**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In an energy-level diagram for an exothermic reaction, which of the following is true regarding the positions of the reactants and products?

options.A: Reactants are at a lower energy level than products.
options.B: Reactants and products are at the identical energy level.
options.C: Reactants are at a higher energy level than products.
options.D: The enthalpy change ($$\Delta H$$) is positive.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze exothermic thermodynamics**
In an exothermic reaction, heat is released because the reactants possess more total chemical potential energy than the products ($$H_{\text{reactants}} > H_{\text{products}}$$).

**Step 2: Relate to the energy diagram**
Therefore, on the vertical y-axis (Enthalpy/Energy), the reactants are positioned **higher** than the products.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct statement is **Reactants are at a higher energy level than products.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In the hypothetical reaction: $$ X_2 + Y_2 \rightarrow 2XY + \text{Heat} $$

options.A: $$ \Delta H $$ is positive and the reaction is endothermic.
options.B: $$ \Delta H $$ is positive and the reaction is exothermic.
options.C: $$ \Delta H $$ is negative and the reaction is endothermic.
options.D: $$ \Delta H $$ is negative and the reaction is exothermic.
options.E: $$ \Delta H $$ may be positive or negative.

cards.why: When '+ Heat' is written on the product side of an equation, it means heat is being **released**. This defines an **exothermic** reaction. In exothermic reactions, the change in enthalpy (**$$ \Delta H $$**) is always **negative**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The stored energy contained in a substance is called
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define the types of energy.**
- Kinetic energy is energy of motion.
- Thermal energy is related to temperature.
- **Chemical energy** is the potential energy stored in the chemical bonds of a substance.

**Result:** Stored energy in a substance is chemical energy.

lessons.title: Types of Heat of Reaction and Heat Changes

cards.title: Types of Heat of Reaction and Heat Changes
body: Main types: heat of combustion, solution, neutralisation, formation, fusion, vaporisation. Thermochemical equation prints ΔH next to the balanced reaction. Units: kJ / kJ mol⁻¹.

cards.title: Types of heat of reaction, step by step
body: Each “heat of …” is ΔH for a stated process and a stated amount — usually **1 mol** of the substance named. Read the definition carefully: it tells you what goes on the left and right of the equation.
**Heat of combustion:** heat released when **1 mol** of a substance burns **completely** in oxygen. Always **negative**. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ/mol.
**Heat of solution:** enthalpy change when **1 mol** of a substance dissolves in a large amount of water. Can be **negative** (NaOH, about −44 kJ/mol) or **positive** (NH₄NO₃, about +26 kJ/mol).

**Heat of neutralisation:** heat released when an acid and a base react to form **1 mol of water**. For any strong acid + strong base: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔH = **−57.1 kJ/mol**. A weak acid gives a smaller value because some energy is used to ionise it.

**Heat of formation:** enthalpy change when **1 mol of a compound** forms from its **elements** in their standard states. C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393 kJ/mol; C(s) + 2S(s) → CS₂(l), ΔH = +117 kJ/mol. The heat of formation of an element is zero.
**Heat of fusion:** heat **absorbed** when 1 mol of solid melts at its melting point. H₂O(s) → H₂O(l), ΔH = +6.01 kJ/mol.
**Heat of vaporisation:** heat **absorbed** when 1 mol of liquid turns into vapour at its boiling point. H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), ΔH = +40.7 kJ/mol.

cards.title: Worked example: heat of neutralisation
cards.problem: 50 mL of 1.0 M HCl is mixed with 50 mL of 1.0 M NaOH. How much heat is released? (ΔH neutralisation = −57.1 kJ/mol)

steps.text: Moles of H⁺ = \(1.0 \times 0.050 = 0.050\text{ mol}\); moles of OH⁻ = 0.050 mol

cards.title: Worked example: which type is it?
cards.problem: Name the type of heat change: (a) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −286 kJ; (b) KOH(aq) + HNO₃(aq) → KNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l), ΔH = −57.1 kJ; (c) H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), ΔH = +40.7 kJ.

steps.text: (a) 1 mol of a compound (water) from its elements → **heat of formation** of water. (It is also the heat of combustion of hydrogen — 1 mol of H₂ burns.)
(b) Acid + base → 1 mol water → **heat of neutralisation**.

cards.answer: (a) formation (= combustion of H₂); (b) neutralisation; (c) vaporisation

cards.title: Memory trick: changes of state
body: **Melting, boiling, evaporating, subliming take heat IN (+). Freezing, condensing take heat OUT (−).** Think of an ice cube melting in your hand: your hand feels cold because the ice takes heat in.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The heat of combustion of a substance is always …
cards.why: Burning releases heat, so ΔH of combustion is always negative.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The heat of neutralisation of any strong acid by any strong base is about −57.1 kJ/mol because …

options.B: the reaction is always H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O

cards.why: Strong acids and bases are fully ionised; the other ions are spectators, so the only reaction is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

cards.title: Tips
body: Check the “1 mol of …” in each definition: combustion = 1 mol of fuel; formation = 1 mol of compound; neutralisation = 1 mol of water.
Heats of fusion and vaporisation are **positive**; the reverse changes (freezing, condensing) have the same numbers with a **negative** sign.
Always give the sign and the unit (kJ/mol) with a ΔH value.

cards.title: Exo I exit heat. Endo I enter heat.
body: The flask of an exo reaction feels hot. Endo feels cold. Photosynthesis stores; combustion spends.

cards.title: Drawing and using energy diagrams
body: Sketch two horizontal lines (reactants, products) and a hump (Ea). If products sit lower, shade ΔH downward and write “exo, ΔH < 0”. If products sit higher, ΔH upward, endo. A catalyst cuts the hump, not the gap between the two lines.

Heat of combustion is usually quoted per mole of fuel burnt completely to CO₂ and H₂O. Heat of neutralisation for strong acid + strong base is about the same number every time because the reaction is really H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. Heat of formation is ΔH when 1 mol of compound is made from elements in their standard states.

When you compare fuels, divide heat released by mass (or by price) — a bigger mole ΔH is not automatically the better cooking fuel if the molecule is huge. Always check the state symbols: extra energy is hidden if a product is steam rather than liquid water.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The stored chemical energy inside a covalent molecular substance, which exists within the chemical bonds holding its atoms together, is classified as what kind of energy?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define energy types**
*   Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.
*   Potential energy is stored energy due to position, composition, or chemical bonds.

**Step 2: Conclusion**
Chemical energy stored within the molecular bonds of a substance is a form of **potential energy**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following constant relationships is correct for converting heat energy units from calories to Joules?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall unit conversion factors**
By standard chemical definition:
$$1\text{ calorie (cal)} = 4.184\text{ Joules (J)} \approx 4.2\text{ Joules (J)}$$

**Step 2: Final Answer**
The correct relationship is **$$1\text{ calorie} = 4.2\text{ Joules}$$**.

cards.title: Exam question, solved
cards.problem: The energy produced due to the motion of the particles of a substance is an example of  A) solar energy.  B) kinetic energy.  C) mechanical energy.  D) potential energy.  E) thermal energy.

steps.text: **Step 1.** **Thermal energy** is the energy contained within a system that is responsible for its temperature.
**Step 2.** It arises from the internal **kinetic energy (motion)** of the atoms and molecules making up the substance.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The heat change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen is called the ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Different reactions have named heat changes.

**Step 2:** Burning one mole completely in oxygen gives the heat of combustion, which is always exothermic (negative ΔH).

**Step 3:** Neutralisation involves an acid and a base; solution involves dissolving.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

tips.text: Energy is a property of matter that allows work to be done.
Temperature is the measure of the hotness or coldness of an object.
The breaking of bonds requires or absorbs energy;the formation of bonds releases energy.
The average energy required to break a chemical bond is called the bond energy. Some salts dissolve endothermically; they require an input of energy for dissolving.

questions.answer: Heat given out to the surroundings. ΔH negative.
why: In an exothermic reaction energy is released to the surroundings, which get warmer; the products have less energy than the reactants, so ΔH is negative.
questions.label: 1. Exothermic means?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: All are correct about an exothermic reaction, except  A) ΔH is negative.  B) the products have less heat energy than the reactants.  C) heat is given off to the environment.  D) energy of the vessel becomes cooler because energy is released.  E) None of the above.
similar.a: D. energy of the vessel becomes cooler because energy is released. — Because heat is released, the vessel and its surroundings become WARMER, not cooler. D is false. Answer: D.

why: In an endothermic reaction energy is absorbed from the surroundings, which get colder; the products have more energy than the reactants, so ΔH is positive.
questions.label: 2. Endothermic means?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: In the hypothetical reaction: X₂ + Y₂ → 2XY + Heat  A) ΔH is positive and the reaction is endothermic.  B) ΔH is positive and the reaction is exothermic.  C) ΔH is negative and the reaction is endothermic.  D) ΔH is negative and the reaction is exothermic.  E) ΔH may be positive or negative.
similar.a: D. ΔH is negative and the reaction is exothermic. — The products have less enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH is negative. Answer: D.

why: Energy must be supplied to pull bonded atoms apart, so breaking bonds is always endothermic.
questions.label: 3. Bond breaking is always?

why: Burning methane releases a lot of heat (ΔH ≈ −890 kJ/mol); that is why it is used as a fuel.
questions.label: 5. Combustion of methane is?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: During exothermic reaction,  A) heat is absorbed.  B) temperature of the vessel decreases.  C) heat of the products is greater than that of the reactants.  D) heat of the reactants is greater than that of the products.  E) A and C.
similar.a: D. heat of the reactants is greater than that of the products. — The released heat is the difference H(reactants) − H(products); therefore the reactants have more heat content than the products (ΔH < 0). Answer: D.

questions.q: Thermal decomposition of carbonate is often?
why: Breaking down a carbonate (e.g. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂) needs continuous heating — energy is taken in, so it is endothermic.
questions.label: 6. Thermal decomposition of carbonate is often?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Photosynthesis is an example of ______ reaction.  A) condensation  B) endothermic  C) exothermic  D) neutralization  E) decomposition
similar.a: B. endothermic — A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings is endothermic (photosynthesis, which makes sugar using energy from sunlight, is an example). Answer: B.

why: When an acid neutralises a base, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O releases heat (about −57 kJ per mole of water), so the mixture warms up.
